Patellar tendinitis is lower confidence because it usually causes anterior focal tenderness without significant global swelling or effusion; isolated tendinopathy rarely produces prominent joint swelling unless complicated by peritendinous inflammation or coexisting pathology. Critical next steps include knee aspiration for cell count, crystals, and culture; CRP/ESR; and imaging if indicated."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Reactive arthritis", "confidence": 0.92}, {"diagnosis": "Septic arthritis", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Gonococcal arthritis", "confidence": 0.81}, {"diagnosis": "Psoriatic arthritis", "confidence": 0.68}, {"diagnosis": "Ankylosing spondylitis with peripheral arthritis", "confidence": 0.62}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.542, "reasoning": "The triad of acute monoarticular knee swelling/pain, low-grade fever (38°C), and antecedent genitourinary symptoms (dysuria for 3 weeks) strongly suggests reactive arthritis—classically triggered by Chlamydia trachomatis infection, which commonly presents with asymptomatic or mild urethritis and subsequent HLA-B27–associated sterile inflammatory arthritis. Septic arthritis remains high-probability due to fever and acute joint inflammation, though absence of systemic toxicity or immunocompromise lowers likelihood slightly; urgent aspiration is mandatory to exclude. Gonococcal arthritis is highly plausible given the dysuria and acute oligoarticular presentation—Neisseria gonorrhoeae frequently causes migratory tenosynovitis/arthritis with minimal constitutional symptoms and may precede or accompany urethritis. Psoriatic arthritis is considered due to the asymmetric lower-limb predominance and possible enthesitis pattern, though absence of skin/nail findings or dactylitis reduces confidence. Ankylosing spondylitis is included as a chronic spondyloarthropathy that can present with acute peripheral arthritis (especially knee) and concomitant urethritis, but typically has insidious onset and back pain—less consistent with 12-day acuity, hence lower confidence."}

Septic arthritis remains high-probability due to acute onset, fever, and monoarticular joint involvement, though absence of reported warmth or systemic toxicity slightly lowers relative likelihood. Gonococcal arthritis is highly plausible given the dysuria and acute inflammatory knee presentation in a sexually active adult; it often presents with migratory tenosynovitis or dermatologic findings not yet queried, but early monoarticular involvement occurs. Psoriatic arthritis is reasonable given enthesitis-like presentation and possible GU inflammation (\"inflammatory arthritis associated with spondyloarthropathy\"), though lack of skin/nail or dactylitis history reduces confidence. Crystal-induced arthritis is less likely: gout typically presents more acutely (<24–72h), lacks prominent dysuria as a trigger, and is less commonly associated with prolonged urinary symptoms; pseudogout usually affects older adults and is less linked to GU inflammation—though not excluded without imaging or synovial fluid analysis."}
